title: A Simple Way To Improve Listening
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin's core prescription is blunt: when students are doing an activity, the teacher should stop talking. He argues most teachers narrate students through nearly every transition and task with a steady stream of reminders and instructions, which trains students not to listen the first time because they know guidance will keep coming. The fix is to move all instruction to before the activity, while students are seated and listening, then give one signal to begin and go fully silent, limiting the teacher's role during the activity itself to observing whether it's done correctly and reteaching afterward if it isn't. He connects this shift to broader claims about learned helplessness, arguing that constant adult narration has stripped students of agency, and lists concrete benefits (better listening, stronger independence, improved behavior) that follow from the change. He acknowledges the transition is harder midyear than at the start of the school year, warning that students accustomed to constant guidance may initially freeze or struggle, but argues persistence pays off substantially.
points: Move all instructions to before an activity begins, while students are seated and listening -- then give one signal and stop talking entirely once they start.
Constant narration during activities (reminders, hints, repeated instructions) trains students not to listen the first time, since they know more guidance is coming.
During the activity, the teacher's only job is to observe silently; getting it wrong is a signal to reteach afterward, not to interject in the moment.
Frames constant adult narration as a driver of learned helplessness that strips students of agency and independence over time.
Warns the shift is harder mid-year than at the start of the year -- students used to constant guidance may initially freeze, but persistence pays off.
quotes: Most teachers—yes, most—talk students through just about everything.
None of it is good for students—because if they know that you’re going to guide them through every activity, transition, etc., then they’re not going to listen to you the first time.
So the solution is to give clear instructions while students are sitting and listening. So, before the actual doing. Then give one signal to begin.
Their responsibility is to perform. Yours is to observe and ensure it’s done as taught. That’s it. You watch but don’t talk.
Furthermore, you stop the slide and scourge of learned helplessness. They’re helpless because the adults in their life have made them that way.

Midyear, however, it may take some time, especially if you’re new to teaching this way. At first, your students will be rattled or even frozen in place. Some will even have trouble putting one foot in front of the other.
